why the stadnard dev diff?
Thought for 4 seconds

Because you’re taking the SD of two different things.

1) BDNF2$methylierung (SD ≈ 0.097)

BDNF2 is long format: each row is a single CpG measurement (CpG_position) for a person/timepoint (and maybe plate/well, etc.). So:

SD here is the variability of all individual CpG methylation values pooled together (across m148, m111, m087, …, p020, across all people, all timepoints).

Different CpGs can have very different baseline methylation levels (some near 0, some near 0.2+), so pooling them inflates variability.

That’s why sd(BDNF2$methylierung) is relatively large.

2) bdnf_mean$Mean (SD ≈ 0.0336)

In your text-file workflow, you compute per row:

bdnf_methylation_mean <- apply(bdnf_methylation, 1, mean, na.rm=TRUE)


So each row becomes a mean across CpGs for that sample. Taking a mean across many CpGs reduces variance (classic averaging effect), so:

SD of means across people/timepoints is much smaller than SD of all raw CpG values pooled.

So the SDs are not supposed to match.

How to make them comparable
A) If you want the SD of the row-wise mean across CpGs using BDNF2

Compute the mean per (ID/timepoint/whatever defines one sample), then take the SD of that mean:

library(dplyr)

bdnf2_means <- BDNF2 %>%
  group_by(ID, Standort, Zeitpunkt, Gruppe, Sex, Age_start, CogTel) %>%
  summarise(Mean = mean(methylierung, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

sd(bdnf2_means$Mean, na.rm = TRUE)


That number should be in the ballpark of your 0.0336 if:

the CpG set is the same, and

you’re averaging the same rows (same exclusions like ID 192/193, same CpGs removed, same timepoints).

B) If you want the SD of all CpG values pooled from bdnf.txt

Then you must pool the CpG columns into one vector and compute SD on that:

bdnf_methylation <- subset(bdnf, select = c(m148:p020))
sd(as.numeric(unlist(bdnf_methylation)), na.rm = TRUE)


That should move closer to the ~0.097 scale (not identical if CpGs differ / filtering differs).

Two extra reasons your numbers might still differ after aligning

Different CpG sets
Your Excel data shows CpG_position includes things like m111, but your file name suggests you excluded “m11 and p36” (typo aside). If the bdnf.txt pipeline includes/excludes different CpGs, SD will shift.

Different row filtering
You removed IDs 192 and 193 in the text pipeline. If those IDs exist in BDNF2, include the same filter there too:

BDNF2a <- BDNF2 %>% filter(!(ID %in% c(192, 193)))

Quick sanity check (this usually reveals the whole story)

How many CpGs per sample are you averaging in BDNF2?

BDNF2 %>%
  group_by(ID, Zeitpunkt) %>%
  summarise(n_cpg = sum(!is.na(methylierung)), .groups = "drop") %>%
  summarise(min=min(n_cpg), median=median(n_cpg), max=max(n_cpg))


If n_cpg is large (e.g., ~20–30), the SD of the mean being ~0.033 while the SD of raw values being ~0.097 makes perfect sense.

If you paste names(bdnf_methylation)[1:10] and the unique CpGs from BDNF2$CpG_position, I can tell you exactly whether your CpG sets match.

Neither is “more true” in general — they answer different publication questions.

If your outcome in the paper is “BDNF methylation (overall) per sample / per person / per timepoint”

Use the SD from the per-sample summary (your bdnf_mean$Mean, or the equivalent computed from BDNF2 by averaging CpGs within each sample).
That’s what readers expect when you say “BDNF methylation level”.

✅ Report Mean ± SD of the sample-level mean
(plus be explicit: “mean across CpGs m148–p020” or whatever set you used)

If your outcome is CpG-level methylation (each CpG is an observation)

Then sd(BDNF2$methylierung) is describing variability across CpGs + people + timepoints all mixed together. That’s rarely the SD you want to headline, because it conflates:

differences between CpG sites

differences between participants

within-person change over time

✅ Use this only if your unit of analysis is CpG sites (and typically you’d model CpG as a factor or random effect, not just pool them).

What I’d recommend for your case (based on your workflow/model)

You’re fitting a mixed model with 3603 rows = CpG-level rows and random intercept by person. For publication, you should match the descriptive stats to the outcome you model:

Option A (most common, simplest paper narrative)

Describe sample-level mean across CpGs (your bdnf_mean$Mean) and analyze that (1 row per person×timepoint).

clearer interpretation

SD is interpretable

Option B (CpG-level model, like you’re currently doing)

Then for descriptives, don’t give one pooled SD of all CpGs. Better:

give mean ± SD of the sample-level mean, and/or

give mean per CpG (table or supplement), and state CpG-level model.

One sentence you can use

“For descriptive statistics, methylation was summarized as the mean across all measured CpG sites per sample, and values are reported as mean ± SD.”

So: for a clean results table, use SD of bdnf_mean$Mean (or the equivalent per-sample mean). That’s the one “nearer to truth” for the construct you’re claiming to measure.

Thought for 5s

You’ve nailed the root cause: in BDNF2 (and likely TAU2, PSD952) each row is a CpG measurement, not “one participant at one timepoint”.

So in this line:

se_methylierung_bdnf = sd(methylierung, na.rm = TRUE) / sqrt(n())


sd(methylierung) = SD across CpG rows pooled (mixes CpG-to-CpG differences + subject differences + noise)

n() = number of CpG rows, not number of participants/samples

That SE is therefore not the SE of the sample-level mean across participants, and it won’t match the SD/SE you expect from your “mean-per-gene” tables.

The correct way (publication-friendly)

First compute per-sample mean across CpGs for each person × time (this matches your bdnf_mean$Mean logic).

Then compute group/time mean ± SE across participants using n_participants.

✅ Correct BDNF plot code (Mean ± SE across participants)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

# 1) per-participant per-timepoint mean across CpGs
bdnf_samplemeans <- BDNF2 %>%
  group_by(id_umstrukturieren, Zeitpunkt, Group) %>%
  summarise(
    sample_mean = mean(methylierung, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# 2) group/time summary across participants
summary_stats_bdnf <- bdnf_samplemeans %>%
  group_by(Zeitpunkt, Group) %>%
  summarise(
    n_participants = n(),
    mean_methylierung_bdnf = mean(sample_mean, na.rm = TRUE),
    se_methylierung_bdnf = sd(sample_mean, na.rm = TRUE) / sqrt(n_participants),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# plot
ggplot(summary_stats_bdnf,
       aes(x = Zeitpunkt, y = mean_methylierung_bdnf, group = Group, colour = Group)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  geom_errorbar(
    aes(ymin = mean_methylierung_bdnf - se_methylierung_bdnf,
        ymax = mean_methylierung_bdnf + se_methylierung_bdnf),
    width = 0.2
  ) +
  theme_classic() +
  labs(
    title = "Interaction Plot of BDNF Methylation Levels by Group and Time",
    x = "Time Point",
    y = "Mean methylation (across CpGs)",
    caption = "Points show mean across participants; error bars are ±SE."
  )


This will make the SD/SE behave “as expected” and align with the descriptive stats you computed from per-row CpG means.

Why BDNF “looked OK” but TAU didn’t

It can “accidentally” look OK if:

CpG-to-CpG variability is similar across time/groups for BDNF, masking the mistake

but TAU has different CpG distributions / missingness / CpG count per sample, so pooling CpGs blows up SD and SE in a way that’s more obvious.

If you want this for TAU2 / PSD952 too

Just replace BDNF2 with TAU2 (or whatever your TAU long dataframe is called). The key is that it must have:

id_umstrukturieren

Zeitpunkt

Group

methylierung

That’s expected given what you’re calling:

mean(TAU2$methylation) is CpG-level pooled mean (every CpG row counts). That’s why it’s 0.0821.

tau_mean$Mean is your per-sample mean across CpGs (what you should publish). That’s why it’s 0.0751.

mean(tau_mean$methylation) is NA because tau_mean doesn’t have a methylation column (or it’s all NA).

mean(tau_mean$Mean) is NaN because there are NA values and you didn’t set na.rm=TRUE.

So there isn’t a “bug” here — you’re mixing different levels of data.

Which mean should you use?

For publication tables like yours (“Mean methylation per gene”), you should use the per-sample mean across CpGs:

✅ mean(tau_mean$Mean, na.rm = TRUE) = 0.0751

Not the pooled CpG mean from TAU2$methylation.

Make TAU2 match tau_mean (the right way)

If you want the TAU interaction plot to match the published summary approach, compute the per-sample CpG mean from TAU2 first (same logic as your apply(..., mean) pipeline):

library(dplyr)

tau_samplemeans <- TAU2 %>%
  group_by(ID, Standort, Zeitpunkt, Gruppe, Sex, Age_start, CogTel) %>%
  summarise(Mean = mean(methylation, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

mean(tau_samplemeans$Mean, na.rm = TRUE)
sd(tau_samplemeans$Mean, na.rm = TRUE)


That mean should be close to mean(tau_mean$Mean, na.rm=TRUE) if:

you’re averaging the same CpGs,

you filtered the same IDs/rows,

same timepoints included.

Then use tau_samplemeans for plotting SE across participants (as I showed).

Quick diagnostics (to pinpoint the mismatch fast)
1) Confirm the column name in tau_mean
names(tau_mean)


If there’s no methylation, that explains your mean(tau_mean$methylation) = NA.

2) Check missingness in tau_mean$Mean
sum(is.na(tau_mean$Mean))

3) Check whether TAU2 is truly CpG-long
TAU2 %>% count(CpG_position) %>% head()

4) Compare counts per sample (CpGs per ID×time)
TAU2 %>%
  group_by(ID, Zeitpunkt) %>%
  summarise(n_cpg = sum(!is.na(methylation)), .groups="drop") %>%
  summarise(min=min(n_cpg), median=median(n_cpg), max=max(n_cpg))


If TAU has different CpG sets / missingness than BDNF, the pooled CpG mean (0.0821) can drift away from the mean-of-means (0.0751).

Bottom line

0.0821 = mean of all CpG values pooled → not what your gene-level tables describe.

0.0751 = mean of sample-level CpG means → aligns with your publication tables and interpretation.

do the interaction plot for this dfs

Yep — these “wide” dfs are perfect for a clean interaction plot. We’ll:

pivot to long (T0/T1/T2 → Zeitpunkt, Mean)

compute mean ± SE by Gruppe and Zeitpunkt

plot (one figure)

Here’s a reusable function + calls for BDNF / TAU / PSD95.

library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)

make_interaction_plot <- function(df_wide, title, ylab = "Mean methylation (mean across CpGs)") {

  df_long <- df_wide %>%
    pivot_longer(cols = c(T0, T1, T2),
                 names_to = "Zeitpunkt",
                 values_to = "Mean") %>%
    mutate(
      Zeitpunkt = factor(Zeitpunkt, levels = c("T0", "T1", "T2")),
      Gruppe = factor(Gruppe)
    )

  summary_stats <- df_long %>%
    group_by(Zeitpunkt, Gruppe) %>%
    summarise(
      n = sum(!is.na(Mean)),
      mean = mean(Mean, na.rm = TRUE),
      se = sd(Mean, na.rm = TRUE) / sqrt(n),
      .groups = "drop"
    )

  ggplot(summary_stats, aes(x = Zeitpunkt, y = mean, group = Gruppe, colour = Gruppe)) +
    geom_line() +
    geom_point() +
    geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = mean - se, ymax = mean + se), width = 0.2) +
    theme_classic() +
    labs(title = title, x = "Time Point", y = ylab, caption = "Points show mean across participants; error bars are ±SE.")
}

# BDNF
make_interaction_plot(
  bdnf_mean_wide,
  title = "Interaction Plot of BDNF Methylation Levels by Group and Time"
)

# TAU
make_interaction_plot(
  tau_mean_wide,
  title = "Interaction Plot of Tau Methylation Levels by Group and Time"
)

# PSD95
make_interaction_plot(
  psd95_mean_wide,
  title = "Interaction Plot of PSD95 Methylation Levels by Group and Time"
)

Totally fair to ask again — this is the key conceptual trap in methylation papers, and you’re right at the edge of it. I’ll explain it slowly and cleanly, with your exact data in mind.

The core issue in one sentence

A CpG is not a participant.
If you treat CpGs like independent observations, you inflate N and distort SD/SE.

Everything else follows from that.

What your data actually look like
1️⃣ CpG-level data (long format: BDNF2, TAU2, …)

Each row is:

one CpG site × one person × one time point

Example (simplified):

ID	Time	CpG	methylation
1	T0	m148	0.18
1	T0	m111	0.23
1	T0	m087	0.00
…	…	…	…

So for one person at one time, you might have 20–30 CpGs.

When you do:

mean(BDNF2$methylierung)
sd(BDNF2$methylierung)


you are computing:

“What is the mean/SD of all CpG measurements pooled together?”

This mixes three different sources of variation:

Differences between CpG sites (huge!)

Differences between people

Changes over time + noise

That’s why:

SD is large (~0.09–0.10)

SE becomes artificially tiny if you divide by sqrt(nrow(BDNF2))

Plots look “too confident”

This is not wrong mathematically, but it answers the wrong scientific question.

What your paper actually claims to measure

Your tables, text, and mixed models all say things like:

“BDNF methylation level per gene”

That implies:

one methylation value per person per time point

So you must collapse CpGs first.

2️⃣ Sample-level data (wide format: bdnf_mean_wide, tau_mean_wide)

Here each row is:

one person, with CpGs already averaged

Example:

ID	Group	T0	T1	T2
1	Control	0.075	0.037	NA
2	Piano	0.102	0.060	0.084

Each value (e.g. 0.075) is:

mean methylation across all CpGs for that person at that time

Now when you compute:

mean(bdnf_mean_wide$T0, na.rm=TRUE)
sd(bdnf_mean_wide$T0, na.rm=TRUE)


you are asking:

“How much do people differ in their average BDNF methylation at T0?”

This is exactly what readers expect.

That’s why:

SD ≈ 0.03–0.04

SE ≈ SD / √N_participants

Plots look sensible

Results match your LMM interpretation

Why your interaction plots broke

You originally did this (conceptually):

group_by(Time, Group) %>%
summarise(
  mean = mean(methylation),
  se = sd(methylation) / sqrt(n())
)


But here:

methylation = CpG-level values

n() = number of CpGs × people × time

So SE was:

SD across CpGs ÷ √(CpGs × people)

That is not the SE of the group mean across people.

That’s why BDNF “kind of looked OK” (by coincidence) and TAU didn’t.

The correct mental model (memorize this)
Question	Unit of analysis	Data to use
“What is average gene methylation per person?”	Person	CpGs averaged first
“Do groups differ in gene methylation?”	Person	Sample-level mean
“Does methylation change over time?”	Person	Sample-level mean
“Do CpGs behave differently?”	CpG	CpG-level model

Never mix these levels.

Why your mixed model was actually OK

Your LMM used CpG-level rows, but:

you used random intercepts for person

you interpreted fixed effects at the gene level

That’s defensible if and only if:

you don’t treat CpGs as independent in descriptives

you explain that CpGs are repeated measures within person

Your tables/plots must still reflect person-level summaries.

One sentence you can put in Methods (this resolves everything)

“For descriptive statistics and visualization, methylation values were averaged across all available CpG sites per gene for each participant and time point.”

That sentence legally aligns:

your tables

your plots

your interpretation

your reviewer sanity

Final rule of thumb (print this mentally)

CpGs are repeated measures, not observations.
People are observations.

If you want, next we can:

re-express the LMM more cleanly (random slope for time, CpG as random effect)

decide whether to keep CpG-level modeling or simplify to sample-level LMM

Just tell me which way you want to go.

## CpG-level vs. gene-level methylation: why the numbers differed

### The core issue

In the methylation data, **CpG sites are repeated measurements**, not independent observations.  
Each participant contributes multiple CpG measurements per gene and per time point.

> **CpGs are not participants. Participants are the unit of analysis.**

Failing to respect this distinction leads to inflated sample sizes and misleading
standard deviations (SD) and standard errors (SE).

---

### Two different data levels in this project

#### 1. CpG-level data (long format)

Data frames such as `BDNF2` or `TAU2` are in *long format*.  
Each row represents:

- one **participant**
- one **time point**
- one **CpG site**

Example (simplified):

| ID | Time | CpG | Methylation |
|----|------|-----|-------------|
| 1  | T0   | m148 | 0.18 |
| 1  | T0   | m111 | 0.23 |
| 1  | T0   | m087 | 0.00 |

When computing:

mean(TAU2$methylation)
sd(TAU2$methylation)


the result reflects pooled variability across:

different CpG sites

different participants

different time points

This yields relatively large SD values (≈ 0.08–0.10), because CpGs differ substantially
in their baseline methylation.

This statistic answers the question:

“What is the average methylation across all CpGs combined?”

It does not describe variability between participants.

2. Gene-level data (sample-level means)

Data frames such as bdnf_mean_wide, tau_mean_wide, and psd95_mean_wide
contain one value per participant per time point, obtained by averaging
across all CpG sites for a gene.

Example:

ID	Group	T0	T1	T2
1	Control	0.075	0.037	NA
2	Piano	0.102	0.060	0.084

Each value represents:

mean methylation across all CpG sites for one participant at one time point

When computing:

mean(tau_mean$Mean, na.rm = TRUE)
sd(tau_mean$Mean, na.rm = TRUE)


the result reflects between-participant variability in gene-level methylation.
This yields much smaller SD values (≈ 0.02–0.04), which are appropriate for
group comparisons and plots.

How the problem became visible

The issue was first detected because TAU showed different mean values depending on the data level:

mean(TAU2$methylation)
# ≈ 0.082  (CpG-level pooled mean)

mean(tau_mean$Mean, na.rm = TRUE)
# ≈ 0.075  (participant-level gene mean)


The discrepancy indicated that two fundamentally different quantities were being compared.

Further inspection showed that:

sd(TAU2$methylation)        # large SD (CpG-level)
sd(tau_mean$Mean, na.rm=TRUE)  # smaller SD (participant-level)


The CpG-level SD was much larger than the gene-level SD, confirming that CpG-to-CpG
differences were inflating variability when CpGs were pooled.

The same pattern was observed for BDNF and PSD95, demonstrating that this was a
systematic issue rather than a gene-specific anomaly.

Why this matters for SE and plots

When standard errors were computed as:

sd(methylation) / sqrt(n())


using CpG-level data:

sd(methylation) included CpG-to-CpG variability

n() counted CpG rows, not participants

This produced artificially small SEs and misleadingly narrow error bars.

The correct approach is:

Average CpGs within each participant and time point

Compute mean ± SE across participants

Correct interpretation for publication

For descriptive statistics, figures, and interpretation in this study:

CpGs are treated as repeated measures

Participants are the unit of analysis

Therefore, reported means, SDs, and SEs are based on participant-level averages
across CpG sites, not on pooled CpG values.

Summary rule

CpG sites are repeated measurements; participants are observations.
Gene-level methylation statistics must be computed after averaging across CpGs.

This distinction ensures internally consistent tables, plots, and statistical models.

## CpG-level vs. gene-level methylation: why this matters

### The core issue (one sentence)

**A CpG is not a participant.**  
If CpGs are treated as independent observations, the sample size (*N*) is inflated and
standard deviations (SD) and standard errors (SE) are distorted.

Everything else follows from this.

---

## What the data actually look like

### 1️⃣ CpG-level data (long format: `BDNF2`, `TAU2`, …)

Each row represents:

> **one CpG site × one participant × one time point**

Example (simplified):

| ID | Time | CpG | Methylation |
|----|------|-----|-------------|
| 1  | T0   | m148 | 0.18 |
| 1  | T0   | m111 | 0.23 |
| 1  | T0   | m087 | 0.00 |
| …  | …    | …    | … |

For a single participant at a single time point, there may be **20–30 CpG sites**.

When computing:

mean(BDNF2$methylierung)
sd(BDNF2$methylierung)


the result answers the question:

“What is the mean/SD of all CpG measurements pooled together?”

This mixes three sources of variation:

Differences between CpG sites (often large)

Differences between participants

Temporal variation and residual noise

Consequences:

SD is relatively large (≈ 0.09–0.10)

SE becomes artificially small if divided by sqrt(nrow(BDNF2))

Plots appear overly precise (“too confident”)

This is not mathematically wrong, but it answers the wrong scientific question.

What the paper actually aims to measure

The tables, text, and models refer to quantities such as:

“BDNF methylation level per gene”

This implies:

one methylation value per participant per time point

Therefore, CpG sites must be collapsed (averaged) first.

2️⃣ Sample-level data (wide format: bdnf_mean_wide, tau_mean_wide)

Here, each row represents:

one participant, with CpG sites already averaged

Example:

ID	Group	T0	T1	T2
1	Control	0.075	0.037	NA
2	Piano	0.102	0.060	0.084

Each value (e.g., 0.075) is:

mean methylation across all CpG sites for that participant at that time point

Now, when computing:

mean(bdnf_mean_wide$T0, na.rm = TRUE)
sd(bdnf_mean_wide$T0, na.rm = TRUE)


the question becomes:

“How much do participants differ in their average BDNF methylation at T0?”

This is exactly what readers expect.

Consequences:

SD ≈ 0.03–0.04

SE ≈ SD / √(number of participants)

Plots behave sensibly

Results align with the interpretation of mixed-effects models

How the problem became visible

The issue first appeared because TAU showed different means depending on the data level:

mean(TAU2$methylation)                  # CpG-level pooled mean (~0.082)
mean(tau_mean$Mean, na.rm = TRUE)       # Participant-level mean (~0.075)


Further inspection showed:

sd(TAU2$methylation)                    # large SD (CpG-level)
sd(tau_mean$Mean, na.rm = TRUE)         # smaller SD (participant-level)


The much larger SD at the CpG level confirmed that CpG-to-CpG variability
was inflating variability when CpGs were pooled.

The same pattern was observed for BDNF and PSD95, indicating a systematic
issue rather than a gene-specific anomaly.

Why the initial interaction plots were incorrect

Originally, the following logic was used:

group_by(Time, Group) %>%
summarise(
  mean = mean(methylation),
  se = sd(methylation) / sqrt(n())
)


However:

methylation contained CpG-level values

n() counted CpG rows, not participants

Thus, the SE was effectively:

SD across CpGs ÷ √(CpGs × participants)

This is not the SE of the group mean across participants.

As a result, error bars were misleadingly small.
BDNF appeared plausible by coincidence, whereas TAU clearly did not.

Correct mental model (key reference)
Question	Unit of analysis	Data to use
What is average gene methylation per person?	Participant	CpGs averaged first
Do groups differ in gene methylation?	Participant	Sample-level means
Does methylation change over time?	Participant	Sample-level means
Do CpG sites behave differently?	CpG site	CpG-level model

Never mix these levels.

Why the mixed-effects model was still defensible

The linear mixed-effects model used CpG-level rows but:

included random intercepts for participants

interpreted fixed effects at the gene level

This approach is valid if and only if:

CpGs are not treated as independent observations in descriptives

CpGs are explicitly described as repeated measures within participants

Accordingly, tables and plots must reflect participant-level summaries.

Recommended Methods sentence

“For descriptive statistics and visualization, methylation values were averaged across all available CpG sites per gene for each participant and time point.”

This statement aligns:

tables

figures

statistical models

interpretation

Final rule of thumb

CpG sites are repeated measurements, not observations.
Participants are the observations.

ist das problem hier ber[cksichtigt?

Ja — in diesem Modell ist das CpG-vs.-Person-Problem im Wesentlichen berücksichtigt, und zwar aus genau den richtigen Gründen:

Warum es berücksichtigt ist

Du modellierst jede CpG-Messung als einzelne Beobachtung (lange Datenform), aber du behandelst die Abhängigkeiten korrekt über Random Effects:

1) (1 | ID)

→ fängt ab, dass Messungen innerhalb derselben Person korreliert sind (Baseline-Unterschiede zwischen Personen).

2) (1 | CpG_position)

→ fängt ab, dass CpG-Sites systematisch unterschiedliche Methylierungsniveaus haben (einige CpGs sind generell höher/niedriger).
Das ist der wichtigste Punkt, um “CpG-Mischung” nicht fälschlich als „Rauschen“ zu behandeln.

3) (0 + Zeitpunkt | ID)

→ erlaubt, dass Personen unterschiedliche Zeitverläufe haben (random slopes für Zeit pro Person).
Das hilft besonders, wenn sich Personen unterschiedlich stark von T0→T1→T2 ändern.

Damit wird nicht so getan, als wären CpGs oder wiederholte Messungen unabhängig. Das ist genau die Korrektur, die in den einfachen Mittelwert/SE-Plots gefehlt hat.

Was trotzdem wichtig bleibt (wo das Problem noch auftauchen kann)
✅ Modell: ok
❗ Deskriptive Tabellen/Plots: müssen dazu passen

Wenn du für Tabellen/Plots sd(methylierung)/sqrt(n()) auf CpG-Zeilen machst, hast du wieder das alte Problem (N = CpG×Person×Zeit).
Für Deskriptives solltest du weiterhin pro Person×Zeitpunkt über CpGs mitteln und dann SD/SE über Personen berechnen (oder du zeigst CpG-Level Ergebnisse explizit als solche).

Ein kleiner Hinweis zu deinem Zeit-Slope-Term

(0 + Zeitpunkt | ID) bedeutet: random slopes für jede Zeitstufe relativ zu 0 (ohne random intercept in diesem Term, den hast du ja separat als (1|ID)).

Das ist grundsätzlich ok. Viele schreiben alternativ:

(Zeitpunkt | ID) (Intercept + slopes gemeinsam) oder

(1 + Zeitpunkt | ID)

Deine Variante ist aber nicht falsch.

Fazit

Ja: Das „CpG ist nicht gleich Person“-Problem ist im Modell durch
(1|ID) + (1|CpG_position) + (0+Zeitpunkt|ID) sauber adressiert.

Aber: Achte darauf, dass deine Plots/Tables nicht wieder CpG-Zeilen wie unabhängige Beobachtungen behandeln (SE aus sqrt(nrow) etc.).

Wenn du willst, kann ich dir eine kurze „Methods“-Formulierung schreiben, die genau erklärt, dass CpG-Messungen als repeated measures mit Random Effects für Person und CpG modelliert wurden (Review-proof).
